outcome: A preprint claiming a proof that no bounded-step infinite path exists was posted 16-17 January 2024 and withdrawn within a day when the author found the moat width had been miscomputed; no other paper, computational record, or claim touching this problem has appeared since. The problem remains open.
summary: The Gaussian moat problem (does an infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes exist with bounded consecutive gaps, i.e. can one walk from the origin to infinity through Gaussian primes with bounded step size) remains open. The only relevant written argument found anywhere in or near the window is arXiv:2401.08441, 'On the Gaussian Moat Problem' by Johann Christian Stumpenhusen, which claimed to prove no such bounded-step walk exists. It was submitted 2024-01-16, revised 2024-01-17, and withdrawn the same week -- the author's own comment states 'the width of the moat was not correctly computed.' This preprint predates the frozen revision (2024-01-26) by ten days, so under a strict reading it would be dated pre-window and hence irrelevant/`open_stale`-adjacent; however, because it never actually settled anything (it was retracted almost immediately after posting, before any expert digestion, and specifically because the core computation was wrong), it is best read as an instructive incident rather than a genuine (if stale) resolution, and I classify it as `progress`/`incident` per SS6.1's 'withdrawn AI claim' pattern generalized to any withdrawn claim -- dated to the claim itself. I found no post-2024-01-26 paper, announcement, or computational record touching this problem. Two much older preprints by Madhuparna Das (arXiv:1908.10392, 'A Note on The Gaussian Moat Problem', originally 2019; and arXiv:1901.10016, 'On the Extension of the Gaussian Moat Problem', originally 2019) each received a v2 on 2024-09-06 that is a withdrawal notice -- the author states the theorems in both were incorrect (Theorem 3 in the first does not actually cover all Gaussian primes and includes non-primes; Theorems 1 and 2 in the second conflate infinitude of rational primes with infinitude of higher-dimensional analogues). These are 2019 claims being formally retracted in September 2024, not new mathematics produced in the window, so they don't constitute a window event on their own, though I note them as background. The oft-cited computational record of a moat of width k=sqrt(36) (Tsuchimura, 'Computational Results for Gaussian Moat Problem') dates to 2004/2005 -- far outside the window -- and no larger record was found. No AI system of any kind is mentioned in connection with any of these papers or with the problem generally; all searches for AI/LLM involvement returned nothing relevant.
competing_reading: One could argue the Stumpenhusen preprint's event date (2024-01-16/17) falls entirely before the frozen revision and should therefore be excluded from the record altogether (treated as if it doesn't exist, rather than as `progress`/`incident`), since the rules define `open_stale` for pre-window resolutions but don't explicitly cover a pre-window claim that was withdrawn before the window began and never touched again. Under that reading the correct status would simply be `open` with `no_change_found` true, and the Stumpenhusen episode would be mentioned only as context predating the window. I lean toward `progress`/`incident` because the withdrawal notice itself (the operative fact -- 'the moat width was not correctly computed') and the paper's v2 are both timestamped 2024-01-17, still nine days before the freeze, so even this doesn't move it into the window; this makes the `open`/`no_change_found` reading the more defensible one, and I flag it as the stronger alternative.
what_would_settle_it: Whether the pipeline intends withdrawn pre-window claims to be recorded as `progress`/`incident` (as an instructive episode worth surfacing) or simply excluded as out-of-window noise under strict dating; a clarifying rule or example covering 'claim posted and withdrawn entirely before 26 Jan 2024' would settle it. Absent that, and given the entire episode's dates precede the freeze, the safer classification is `open` with `no_change_found` true.
